1.note: This is a continuation of what Yahweh said to Ezekiel. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh as in the UST.

Yahweh is using **son of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human being.” See the Introduction to Ezekiel for more information on this form of address. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST. See how you translated the same expression in [2:1](ta:02).

1.q: קַח־לְ⁠ךָ֣ לְבֵנָ֔ה וְ⁠נָתַתָּ֥ה אוֹתָ֖⁠הּ לְ⁠פָנֶ֑י⁠ךָ וְ⁠חַקּוֹתָ֥ עָלֶ֛י⁠הָ עִ֖יר אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
1.note: Drawing a picture of the city of Jerusalem on a clay brick and setting it in front of himself was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed the people of Israel that Yahweh was going to send an enemy army to attack their city. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in a footnote.

A **brick** is a kind of block made of clay that has been shaped while it is soft and then dried until it is hard. People of this culture drew and wrote on bricks of this kind while the clay was still soft. If your readers would not be familiar with what a brick is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a soft clay block]

Here, **to your face** represents placing something before you or in front of you. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before your face]

2.note: The implication is that Ezekiel is not to lay an actual siege (surrounding and attacking a fortified place to isolate it from support and supplies, compelling the surrender of those inside) against Jerusalem but to act out a siege against the brick with the picture of the city that he has drawn on it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Then, you shall act out a siege against that brick with the drawing of the city],

A **mound**, in the context of a siege, is a kind of ramp of packed earth that an attacking army piled up against the wall of a city so that its soldiers could climb over the wall. If your readers would not be familiar with what a mound of this kind is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [a ramp of earth]

Here, **camps** represents enemy soldiers gathered in camps around a city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [enemy camps full of soldiers]

The term **battering rams** describes a kind of heavy beam that soldiers swung against the gates or walls of a city in order to break through them. If your readers would not be familiar with what battering rams are, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [heavy beams for smashing through the walls]

3.q: קַח־לְ⁠ךָ֙ מַחֲבַ֣ת בַּרְזֶ֔ל וְ⁠נָתַתָּ֤ה אוֹתָ⁠הּ֙ קִ֣יר בַּרְזֶ֔ל בֵּינְ⁠ךָ֖ וּ⁠בֵ֣ין הָ⁠עִ֑יר
3.note: Setting an iron griddle between himself and the model of the city was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed that Yahweh had placed a barrier between himself and the people of Jerusalem, so that he would no longer answer them when they cried out to him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in a footnote.

A **griddle** is a kind of flat iron plate that people used for baking bread over a fire. If your readers would not be familiar with what a griddle is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [an iron baking pan]

Making one’s face firm was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed Yahweh’s firm resolve and angry purpose against Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in a footnote.

Here, **house of Israel** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also called Israel, and is used here to describe the northern kingdom of Israel. Alternate translation: [for the kingdom of Israel]

4.note: Yahweh is speaking as if **the iniquity of the house of Israel** were a heavy object that Ezekiel could **put** on his own body. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you shall take on the punishment for the house of Israel]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the house of Israel has done wrong]

Here, **house of Israel** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also called Israel, and is used here to describe the northern kingdom of Israel. Alternate translation: [the kingdom of Israel]

Yahweh is using **bear their iniquity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “endure the punishment for what they have done wrong.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will endure the punishment for what they have done wrong]

5.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **years** that are characterized by **their iniquity**, that is, approximately the number of years since Solomon, the first idol-worshiping king of Israel, during which the people of Israel sinned against him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the years during which they sinned]
Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture.
See how you translated these same phrases, “bear the iniquity” and “house of Israel” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [and you shall take on the punishment for the house of Israel]

6.note: See how you translated these similar phrases, “bear the iniquity” and “house of Israel” in 4:4. Alternate translation: [and you shall take on the punishment for the house of Judah]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the guilt for the sins]

Here, **house of Judah** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Judah** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob and is used to describe the southern kingdom of Israel. Alternate translation: [people from the kingdom of Judah]

Yahweh is repeating the phrase **a day for a year** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [exactly one day for each year]

7.note: The implication is that **the siege** mentioned is the model siege that Ezekiel has set up, not an actual siege of the city. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And toward the model siege of Jerusalem that you have set up]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **siege** that is characterized by being directed against **Jerusalem**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the siege against Jerusalem]
See how you translated this same phrase, “shall make firm your face” in 4:3.

The expression **bared** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and you shall bare your arm]

Baring the arm as a warrior would who is preparing to fight was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed that Yahweh was ready to fight against the city. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in a footnote.

8.note: Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listener’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And now listen]
See how you translated the similar expression, “put on you ropes,” in 3:25.

9.q: קַח־לְ⁠ךָ֡ חִטִּ֡ין וּ֠⁠שְׂעֹרִים וּ⁠פ֨וֹל וַ⁠עֲדָשִׁ֜ים וְ⁠דֹ֣חַן וְ⁠כֻסְּמִ֗ים
9.note: The implication is that people of this culture would mix so many different grains and legumes together only when food was scarce, so this bread is a sign of the famine that the siege would bring. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [take for yourself whatever grains you can find—wheat and barley and beans and lentils and millet and rye—as people do when food is scarce]

The terms **beans**, **lentils**, **millet**, and **rye** describe kinds of crops that people of this region grew for food. If your readers would not be familiar with what these crops are, you could use the names of similar crops that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and other grains and seeds]

10.note: These **twenty shekels** of food together came to about 220 grams or about eight ounces. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

Yahweh is using **From time to time** as a common expression of the culture to mean “at set times each day.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [At set times each day, you shall eat it]

11.note: A **hin** was equivalent to about 3.7 liters, so a **sixth** (one part out of six equal parts) of a hin was equivalent to about 0.6 liters or about a pint and a quarter. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “hin” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the approximate measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote..
See how you translated this phrase, “From time to time,” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [At set times throughout the day]

12.note: A **cake of barley** is a kind of flat, round loaf of bread that people could bake over an open fire. If your readers would not be familiar with what a cake of barley is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [And a flat, round loaf]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **dung** that is characterized by being **the excrement of man**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in dung that consists of human excrement]

The pronoun **their** refers to the people of Israel, who will watch Ezekiel as he does this. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the sight of the people of Israel]
Here, **eyes** represents “seeing.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [while they watch]

13.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Israel were literally the **sons** of the patriarch **Israel**. He means that they are his descendants. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

The implication is that this food will be impure or ceremonially **unclean** according to the law that Yahweh gave to Israel, as a sign of the severe defilement and siege conditions the people of Israel will face while they are living among foreign nations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [their food that is impure and ceremonially unclean]
Yahweh is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their unclean food]

14.note: Ezekiel is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of dismay. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Please, no, Lord Yahweh]

Ezekiel is using the term **Behold** as an emphatic way to focus Yahweh’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Please pay attention]

The expression **has not been made unclean** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I have never done anything that would make me unclean]

The implication is that the law that Yahweh gave to Israel did not permit the people to eat the meat of an animal that had died on its own or that a wild animal had killed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers as modeled in the UST.

Ezekiel is using **entered into my mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I have eaten.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I have never consumed meat of defilement]

Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe **meat** that is characterized by **defilement**. This is likely to refer to meat that was meant as a sacrifice and was kept beyond the time prescribed for it to be eaten, or more generally, meat that has become unacceptable to offer or to eat for any reason. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [spoiled meat]

15.note: The implication is that dried cattle droppings were an ordinary fuel that people of this culture used for cooking and that using them would not make Ezekiel or his food unclean. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [cow dung, an ordinary cooking fuel, instead of the excrement of man]

16.note: Yahweh is using **behold me** as a common expression of this culture to mean that he is about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [now I am about to break]

Yahweh is using **breaking the staff of bread** as a common expression of the culture to mean “cutting off the supply of food.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [cutting off the supply of food in Jerusalem]

The implication is that the people of Jerusalem will have to weigh out their food because so little of it will be left during the siege. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they will carefully weigh out the little bread they have left and eat it anxiously]
Here, **bread** represents food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [food]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **anxiety**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [measured out anxiously]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **horror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and while feeling horrified]

17.note: Yahweh is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will lack food]

Yahweh is using **A man and his brother** as a common expression of the culture to mean “every person.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Each person]

The expression **will be dismayed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will feel dismayed]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because they have acted wickedly]
